This agent should be invoked after a TypeScript Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- plugin-dev:agent-creator: Use this agent when the user asks to "create an agent", "generate an agent", "build a new agent", "make me an agent that...", or describes agent functionality they need. Trigger when user wants to create autonomous agents for plugins. Examples:

<example>
Context: User wants to create a code review agent
user: "Create an agent that reviews code for quality issues"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate the agent configuration."
<commentary>
User requesting new agent creation, trigger agent-creator to generate it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User describes needed functionality
user: "I need an agent that generates unit tests for my code"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to create a test generation agent."
<commentary>
User describes agent need, trigger agent-creator to build it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants to add agent to plugin
user: "Add an agent to my plugin that validates configurations"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate a configuration validator agent."
<commentary>
Plugin development with agent addition, trigger agent-creator.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Write, Read)

- plugin-dev:plugin-validator: Use this agent when the user asks to "validate my plugin", "check plugin structure", "verify plugin is correct", "validate plugin.json", "check plugin files", or mentions plugin validation. Also trigger proactively after user creates or modifies plugin components. Examples:

<example>
Context: User finished creating a new plugin
user: "I've created my first plugin with commands and hooks"
assistant: "Great! Let me validate the plugin structure."
<commentary>
Plugin created, proactively validate to catch issues early.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the plugin."
</example>

<example>
Context: User explicitly requests validation
user: "Validate my plugin before I publish it"
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to perform comprehensive validation."
<commentary>
Explicit validation request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified plugin.json
user: "I've updated the plugin manifest"
assistant: "Let me validate the changes."
<commentary>
Manifest modified, validate to ensure correctness.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the manifest."
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- plugin-dev:skill-reviewer: Use this agent when the user has created or modified a skill and needs quality review, asks to "review my skill", "check skill quality", "improve skill description", or wants to ensure skill follows best practices. Trigger proactively after skill creation. Examples:

<example>
Context: User just created a new skill
user: "I've created a PDF processing skill"
assistant: "Great! Let me review the skill quality."
<commentary>
Skill created, proactively trigger skill-reviewer to ensure it follows best practices.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the skill."
</example>

<example>
Context: User requests skill review
user: "Review my skill and tell me how to improve it"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to analyze the skill quality."
<commentary>
Explicit skill review request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified skill description
user: "I updated the skill description, does it look good?"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the changes."
<commentary>
Skill description modified, review for triggering effectiveness.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

## ac642cf1-e1c8-4490-9caa-814476453870
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- playwright-skill: Complete browser automation with Playwright. Auto-detects dev servers, writes clean test scripts to /tmp. Test pages, fill forms, take screenshots, check responsive design, validate UX, test login flows, check links, automate any browser task. Use when user wants to test websites, automate browser interactions, validate web functionality, or perform any browser-based testing.
- audit-tier: Identify the protection tier, owner, and import blast radius of a file or directory under overrides/. Use before editing anything you're unsure about.
- code-quality: Audit recently changed or specified files for code quality issues — naming, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence, and structural debt. Read-only. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR.
- code-review: AI-powered code review using CodeRabbit. Default code-review skill. Trigger for any explicit review request AND autonomously when the agent thinks a review is needed (code/PR/quality/security).
- contentful-register-component: Register a Zimmermann React component with Contentful Studio Experiences. Use when a developer asks to register, add, or expose a React component to Contentful, or when they need to create a Contentful component definition for an existing component.
- feature-spec: Turn a plain-English feature request into a scoped implementation plan before any code is written. Asks one clarifying question at a time, then produces a spec Claude Code can execute safely. Use this before starting any non-trivial implementation session.
- generate-changelog: Generate a release changelog from conventional commits and upstream baseline notes. Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release. Use before cutting a release branch or when preparing release notes.
- new-component: Scaffold a new Zimmermann component under overrides/app/components/ — TypeScript, Chakra-first, with a paired Storybook story. Use whenever a new custom component is needed.
- onboarding: Interactive onboarding for new developers and QA engineers joining the Zimmermann PWA Kit project. Asks role at the start, checks the mechanical setup items, then orients the person to the rules and tools relevant to their role and squad. Run this in the first Claude Code session on a new machine or a first day on the project.
- pr-checklist: Generate a PR description and merge checklist based on the files changed on the current branch. Pairs with /code-quality.
- project-init: One-time project setup walkthrough. Runs the state detection script, fixes automatable items, asks one question at a time for human-input items, and updates the 7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist Confluence page as each item is confirmed. Run this once when setting up the project for the first time, or when returning to check setup status.
- qa-generate: Generate a Gherkin .feature file and Playwright test spec from a Jira story. Human-in-the-lead — Lead QA validates the .feature before Playwright is generated. Use for any new storefront user journey that needs E2E test coverage.
- scope-check: Review a proposed Claude Code prompt for scope safety before it runs. Classifies every likely-touched file by tier and verdicts the prompt SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED, rewriting it when needed.
- session-start: Run the mandatory session start ritual — reads tracking docs, runs branch + health checks, states current position. Use at the start of every coding session.
- upstream-sync-review: Review the release notes / changelog for a new @salesforce/retail-react-app version before bumping. Lightweight policy — see .docs/upstreamPolicy.md.
- agent-sdk-dev:new-sdk-app: Create and setup a new Claude Agent SDK application
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- code-review:code-review: Code review a pull request
- commit-commands:clean_gone: Cleans up all git branches marked as [gone] (branches that have been deleted on the remote but still exist locally), including removing associated worktrees.
- commit-commands:commit-push-pr: Commit, push, and open a PR
- commit-commands:commit: Create a git commit
- feature-dev:feature-dev: Guided feature development with codebase understanding and architecture focus
- plugin-dev:create-plugin: Guided end-to-end plugin creation workflow with component design, implementation, and validation
- pr-review-toolkit:review-pr: Comprehensive PR review using specialized agents
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- vercel:bootstrap: Bootstrap a repository with Vercel-linked resources by running preflight checks, provisioning integrations, verifying env keys, and then executing db/dev startup commands safely.
- vercel:deploy: Deploy the current project to Vercel. Pass "prod" or "production" as argument to deploy to production. Default is preview deployment.
- vercel:env: Manage Vercel environment variables. Commands include list, pull, add, remove, and diff. Use to sync environment variables between Vercel and your local development environment.
- vercel:status: Show the status of the current Vercel project — recent deployments, linked project info, and environment overview.
- claude-code-setup:claude-automation-recommender: Analyze a codebase and recommend Claude Code automations (hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, MCP servers). Use when user asks for automation recommendations, wants to optimize their Claude Code setup, mentions improving Claude Code workflows, asks how to first set up Claude Code for a project, or wants to know what Claude Code features they should use.
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design).     "title": "04.71 Writing User Stories for Components",
    "type": "page",
    "created": "",

    "url": "https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/400195600",

    "content": {
      "value": "### How to write user stories for the Zimmermann build

#### Overview

User stories are organised across two levels: component epics and page epics. Each serves a different purpose and audience.

---

#### Level 1 — Component epics

This is the build story for each individual component. It covers what the component does, its variants and configurations, accessibility requirements, and any error or empty states.

**There are two types of component, and this determines how many stories you write:**

**PWA Kit only** (e.g. Button, Textfield, Dropdown, Cart Item)  
These are functional UI components with no content authoring required. Write one story, in the PWA Kit epic only. No Contentful story is needed.

**Contentful + PWA Kit** (e.g. Banner, Editorial Cards, Footer, Navigation)  
These components have content that an editor manages. Write two stories:

* One in the **Contentful epic** — covering the content model, authoring fields, configuration options and validation rules
* One in the **PWA Kit epic** — covering how the component renders and responds to what Contentful delivers

> A Contentful component always needs a PWA Kit story too, because PWA Kit has to render it. A PWA Kit-only component does not need a Contentful story.

---

#### Level 2 — Page epics

This is the experience story for a specific page (e.g. PDP, PLP, Checkout). Rather than focusing on individual component builds, these stories describe how components work together to deliver a user journey.

Write these from the customer's perspective — for example, on the PDP: a customer selects a size using the size selector, selects a colour using the colour attribute component, and adds the item to their bag using the add to cart component.

These stories should not repeat the component build detail from Level 1. They are about the interaction between components and the end-to-end experience on that page.

---

#### Quick reference

| Level | Epic | Focus | Written from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | PWA Kit component | Build, variants, accessibility | Developer perspective |
| 1 | Contentful component | Content model, authoring, field config | Merchandiser perspective |
| 1 | PWA Kit (render) | Rendering Contentful output | Developer perspective |
| 2 | Page (e.g. PDP) | How components work together | Shopper perspective |",
      "format": "markdown"
    }
  }
}

content.thinking:
I'm spotting a critical mismatch between the two stories — SFCC-698's content model doesn't define a title field, but SFCC-699's acceptance criteria expects one to display on the card alongside the image, body copy, and CTA. That's a contract violation between what Contentful is supposed to provide and what the PWA Kit component is supposed to render.

And I'm noticing something else problematic: AC2 through AC8 in SFCC-698 are actually render assertions ("When the component renders... Then one card displays left-aligned"), not content-model assertions. Those belong in the PWA Kit story, not the Contentful story — this violates the clean separation between the two.

There's also an unresolved question embedded directly in AC1 ("Image (required) - from Contentful for editorial?"), which shouldn't be in acceptance criteria. And AC3 mentions "two cards side by side," but the content model only describes a single card's fields with no collection structure or card-count field — so whether this is a container with a list or individual entries is completely unspecified. The Layout field also conflates two separate concerns that should be orthogonal.

Looking at SFCC-700, there's a clear contradiction where AC3 says "footer above" when the footer is actually below, and the hardcoded pixel values (40px, 16px) violate the repo's own Chakra token rule against using pixel values for spacing — these should reference spacing tokens instead.

The story context also shifts between "shopper browsing product listing page" and the summary/AC treating it as a homepage, which is inconsistent. While the page-level AC does address component assembly and positioning, the focus on specific spacing values feels more like build detail than the journey-focused approach the standard calls for.

SFCC-699 is better structured — the AC around internal vs external CTA link behavior and alt text requirements are well-formed and align with the repo's own accessibility rules.

But there's a standards mismatch I'm noticing: SFCC-648 references WCAG 2.1 AA, while the repo's AGENTS.md targets WCAG 2.2 AA with 2.1 AA only as a fallback when 2.2 is technically infeasible. That's a contradiction worth flagging.

SFCC-699 also has gaps — there's no AC for loading or skeleton states, error handling when Contentful is unavailable (which the repo requires for independent system failures), missing required fields, unpublished entries, or image lazy-loading behavior.…

content.text: Now the codebase side — the actual Contentful↔PWA Kit contract that these stories have to feed.

---
name: contentful-register-component
description: Register a Zimmermann React component with Contentful Studio Experiences. Use when a developer asks to register, add, or expose a React component to Contentful, or when they need to create a Contentful component definition for an existing component.
allowed-tools: Read, Edit, Bash
---

# Contentful Component Registration

Studio Experiences definitions are now **generated from code** — you never write a
`defineComponents` entry by hand. The source of truth is the component's `Props` type,
annotated with `@cf` JSDoc tags.

## Steps

### 1. Move the component into `experiences/`

The codegen only processes files under
`overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/`. If the component isn't there yet,
move it (or create it) in that folder.

### 2. Add `/** @cf-register */` to the component

Place it immediately before the component's `const` declaration:

```tsx
/** @cf-register */
const MyComponent = ({ ... }: MyComponentProps) => { ... };

export default MyComponent;
```

### 3. Annotate every prop in the `Props` type

Props without a `@cf` tag are silently skipped — omitting the tag is how you exclude a prop from the Contentful definition.

```tsx
type MyComponentProps = {
  /** @cf Headline */
  headline: string;

  /** @cf Body Copy, longText */
  body?: string;

  /** @cf Hero Image, media */
  heroImage?: string;

  /** @cf Layout, select */
  layout?: 'left' | 'right';

  internalId?: string;
};
```

**Tag syntax:**

| Tag | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `/** @cf Display Name */` | Infer control from the TS type (see table below) |
| `/** @cf Display Name, control */` | Override the inferred control |

Props without any `@cf` tag are silently skipped — no tag needed to exclude a prop.

**Type → control inference table:**

| TypeScript type | Inferred control | Contentful variable type |
|----------------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| `string` | `shortText` | Text |
| `boolean` | `toggle` | Boolean |
| `number` | `number` | Number |
| string literal union (`'a' \| 'b'`) | `select` | Text |

**Valid explicit controls:** `shortText`, `longText`, `select`, `toggle`, `number`, `media`

**Auto-skipped:** props starting with `on` (event handlers), `children` (emits
`children: true` on the component registration instead), and any prop with no `@cf` tag.

### 4. Run the generator

```bash
npm run generate:contentful
```

This rewrites `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts`
automatically. Verify the output looks correct, then commit both the annotated
component and the updated `definitions.ts`.

### 5. Verify

```bash
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run generate:contentful:check
```

`--check` exits zero if `definitions.ts` is in sync with the source files.

---

## Notes

- **Never edit `definitions.ts` by hand** — it is autogenerated and will be overwritten
  on the next run.
- The pre-commit hook auto-runs the generator whenever an `experiences/*.tsx` file is
  staged, so `definitions.ts` stays in sync automatically.
- `children: ReactNode` → use `children: true` convention; the generator handles this
  automatically when it sees a `children` prop.
- `thumbnailUrl` is left blank until a real Contentful account exists.
- Component `id` is auto-derived as kebab-case of the filename
  (`myComponent.tsx` → `my-component`).
- Component `name` is auto-derived as Title Case of the id words
  (`my-component` → `My Component`).

**Type → control inference table:**

| TypeScript type | Inferred control | Contentful variable type |
|----------------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| `string` | `shortText` | Text |
| `boolean` | `toggle` | Boolean |
| `number` | `number` | Number |
| string literal union (`'a' \| 'b'`) | `select` | Text |

**Valid explicit controls:** `shortText`, `longText`, `select`, `toggle`, `number`, `media`

**Auto-skipped:** props starting with `on` (event handlers), `children` (emits
`children: true` on the component registration instead), and any prop with no `@cf` tag.

### 4. Run the generator

```bash
npm run generate:contentful
```

This rewrites `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts`
automatically. Verify the output looks correct, then commit both the annotated
component and the updated `definitions.ts`.

### 5. Verify

```bash
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run generate:contentful:check
```

`--check` exits zero if `definitions.ts` is in sync with the source files.

---

## Notes

- **Never edit `definitions.ts` by hand** — it is autogenerated and will be overwritten

  staged, so `definitions.ts` stays in sync automatically.
- `children: ReactNode` → use `children: true` convention; the generator handles this

- `thumbnailUrl` is left blank until a real Contentful account exists.
- Component `id` is auto-derived as kebab-case of the filename
  (`myComponent.tsx` → `my-component`).
- Component `name` is auto-derived as Title Case of the id words
  (`my-component` → `My Component`).

37	
38	Content type schemas are managed in code, not in the Contentful UI:
39	
40	- Schema definitions live in the PWA repo and are reviewed via pull request.
41	- A sync script (Management API) idempotently upserts content types into the target environment. The sync script is authored to be additive only — it never deletes a field from a live content type.
42	- Each content type pairs with a typed React component. TypeScript types match the Contentful field IDs exactly, so schema drift is caught at compile time.
43	
44	## 3. Browser-side architecture
45	
46	```
47	PWA (SSR layer, then CSR hydration)
48	        │
49	        ├──► Contentful Delivery API (CDA) — published content
50	        │        SSR fetches server-side; browser also uses CDA on
51	        │        post-hydration reads. Public token, safe in bundle.
52	        │
53	        ├──► Contentful Preview API (CPA) — draft content
54	        │        Editor preview only. Token set in MRT as an env var
55	        │        on dev/test/sit/uat only (never staging or prod).
56	        │        Reached client-side on the /preview route and via
57	        │        ?preview on Experience pages — both are gated: if no
58	        │        CPA token is present, both paths fail explicitly with
59	        │        a 404 and are noindex (no delivery fallback). The Live
60	        │        Preview SDK requires the token in the browser for
61	        │        postMessage-based real-time updates.
62	        │
63	        ├──► Contentful Images API (images.ctfassets.net)
64	        │        srcset / sizes / avif|webp / quality parameters
65	        │
66	        └──◄  Publish webhook → MRT /webhooks/contentful
67	                 Clears affected SSR cache keys on entry publish.
68	                 HMAC-verified with a shared secret.
69	```
70	
71	- **SSR first.** Editorial content for SEO- and LCP-critical pages (homepage, PLP, PDP, campaign landings) is fetched server-side. The browser hydrates from the SSR payload — no CDA call on first paint.
72	- **GraphQL for composed pages.** Where a page assembles many entries the storefront uses the GraphQL Content API to fetch only the needed fields in one request. REST CDA is used for simpler reads.
73	- **Live preview.** When an editor opens preview in Contentful Studio, the `/preview` route renders the entry inside Studio's iframe. The `@contentful/live-preview` SDK subscribes to `postMessage` events from Studio for real-time content updates. The CPA token is used client-side here — this is required by the SDK and is acceptable because: (a) the token is set only on dev/test/sit/uat (never staging or prod) MRT environments, (b) the route returns a 404 when no preview token is present, and (c) the route is `noindex`. The MRT proxy approach was considered but deferred in favour of the simpler client-side SDK integration.
74	- **Asset delivery.** Images come from `images.ctfassets.net`. The storefront generates `srcset`, `sizes`, AVIF with WebP fallback, and quality parameters per breakpoint.
75

77	
78	| Token | Where used | Sensitivity |
79	|---|---|---|
80	| Delivery API token (CDA) | Browser bundle and SSR | Public — read-only, scoped to one environment. Safe to embed. |

content.thinking:
I'm cross-referencing the component inventory against the design stories to verify classifications. Editorial Cards are marked as "Contentful" in the system, though the status isn't yet confirmed, and there are several variants I'm tracking including the two-column and centered text versions.

However, when I look at the actual content model in SFCC-698, it only supports a single layout enum (Standard or Centred text) with no column-count field, which means it can't actually express all four inventory variants. Additionally, the inventory's Pages column is blank for Editorial Cards even though SFCC-698 and SFCC-700 both reference it being used on the homepage and product listing pages.

For the Title and Link component, there's a similar discrepancy—the acceptance criteria in SFCC-698 reference SFCC-691, which is the PWA Kit render story, but the actual Contentful content model is SFCC-692, so the dependencies are pointing to the wrong artifact.

The inventory also uses a third classification, "PWA Kit & Contentful," that doesn't align with the standard 04.71 framework, which only defines "PWA Kit only" and "Contentful + PWA Kit." Since the standard states that every Contentful component needs a corresponding PWA Kit story for rendering, the inventory's single-word "Contentful" labels are ambiguous—they don't clarify whether a PWA Kit story exists alongside them.

Additionally, Footer is classified as "Contentful" in the inventory but its stories are parented to the Homepage epic when Footer is actually a global shell component that should belong to a Shell epic instead, creating a structural misfile in Jira.

Navigation is marked as "Contentful" and does have an epic (SFCC-3), though the epic split appears incomplete with the Language Selector ticket still missing.

The Templates table only documents Shell and PDP, but stories are already being written against Homepage and PLP templates that aren't listed there, and the Pages column lacks mappings for components like Editorial Cards, making it impossible to determine which page epics actually need coverage.

Looking at the technical constraints, Studio Experiences codegen has serious limitations — it only supports Text, Boolean, Number, and Media controls, but SFCC-698 requires a repeating collection of independently configured cards and optional sub-component references that the system can't express. The precedent with `shoppableImage` shows the workaround was forcing merchandisers to write JSON directly, which won't scale for editorial authoring, so Editorial Cards needs a different approach.

The real solution is to leverage the `children: true` composition primitive that Experiences already supports — model this as a container component with two slots, each holding a single Editorial Card component, rather than trying to cram everything into one story with a layout enum. This fundamentally changes the story structure: separate component stories for `editorialCard` and the 2-column container, not a monolithic "Editorial Cards Module" story.

For Experiences components, the authoring fields are generated from React Props via the `@cf` tags, so the dependency flows from code to content model, not the other way around.  That's the opposite of the 04.71 model, which assumes Contentful story feeds PWA Kit story. The standard needs to explicitly call out which mechanism applies — Experiences (code-first) versus content-type components (Contentful-first) — because it changes sequencing, ownership, and what "done" means. And since content-type syncs are additive-only, getting the model wrong is expensive to undo, which makes reviewing the Contentful story against the component's actual capabilities critical.

The real gap is that neither SFCC-698 nor SFCC-699 encodes the field-ID contract as an acceptance criterion. The stories mention display names like "Body copy" but never list the actual field IDs that TypeScript will match against — and that's the artifact that makes the two stories independently workable. Adding a field-ID table to the story template would be the single most useful thing to clarify the interface between Contentful and PWA Kit work.…

99	## 6. Performance and loading strategy
100	
101	- **SSR cache.** Contentful responses are cached at the SSR/edge layer — TTL 60 seconds with stale-while-revalidate. Publish webhooks clear the cache; the TTL is the fallback.
102	- **CDN rate limits.** Contentful allows 55 uncached requests per second per CDA token. The SSR cache absorbs almost all traffic so this limit is only a risk during burst republish events.
103	- **Images.** AVIF with WebP fallback via the Images API. Lazy loading on all below-the-fold images. The largest hero carries `fetchpriority="high"`.
104	- **Preconnect.** `images.ctfassets.net` is preconnected from the document head. `cdn.contentful.com` is not — first paint hydrates from SSR, so no browser CDA call is on the critical path.
105	- **Bundle weight.** The rich-text renderer is dynamically imported only on pages that use rich-text fields.
106	- **Field projection.** GraphQL queries select only the fields the component uses. REST queries use the `select` parameter where supported.
107	
108	## 7. Multi-region behaviour
109	
110	- A single Contentful Space serves all eight storefronts via Contentful's native locale model.
111	- The active locale is resolved from the URL prefix and passed as `locale=` on every CDA request. Eleven active locales: en-AU, en-US, en-GB, en (EU), fr, it, es, en-CH, en-HK, en-AE.
112	- Region-specific entries (banners, promotions, editorial that varies by site) are filtered at query time using the active SFCC site ID.
113	
114	## 8. Failure modes and graceful degradation
115	
116	| Failure | Behaviour |
117	|---|---|
118	| Contentful CDA unavailable | Page renders without editorial content. Editorial slots show empty; commerce data is never blocked on a CMS read. |
119	| Stale cached content after a publish | Tolerated within the 60-second TTL. The publish webhook normally clears affected entries in seconds; the TTL is the safety net if the webhook drops. |
120	| Preview API returns broken or unpublished refs | Editor preview only — render a placeholder. Production traffic never hits this path. |
121	| Asset (image) 404 | Show alt text and a graceful placeholder. |
122	| 429 rate limit on CDA | Exponential backoff and retry. The SSR cache makes this rare in practice. |
123	| Publish webhook fails HMAC verification | Reject and log. Storefront continues serving from cache; the TTL picks up the change. |
124	| Live preview iframe disconnects | Storefront silently returns to non-preview mode. |
125	
126	## 9. Security and privacy
127	
128	- The CDA token is read-only and scoped to one environment. Embedding in the bundle is safe per Contentful's published guidance.
129	- The CPA token is set in MRT on dev/test/sit/uat only — never on staging or prod. It reaches the browser on the `/preview` route and `?preview` Experience pages, both of which return 404 when no token is present. Both preview paths are `noindex` and not linked from any storefront navigation. This is a deliberate tradeoff: the Live Preview SDK requires the token client-side for real-time postMessage updates, and the non-prod-only gate means the token is never in a production bundle.
130	- The CMA token is held only on the CI host — never embedded, never in PR diffs.
131	- No PII is handled by Contentful.
132	
133	## 10. Open items requiring client confirmation
134	
135	1. **`regions` content-model field.** The working assumption is that region-specific entries are filtered by a `regions` field containing the relevant SFCC site IDs. Pending content-strategy and editor-workflow sign-off — this field affects how editors author content across all eight storefronts.
136	2. **SFCC vs Contentful content ownership on composed pages.** The principle is settled — SFCC owns all commerce data, Contentful owns editorial. Not yet confirmed is the split on composed pages: which editorial blocks appear on PDP and PLP, whether they are authored in SFCC Page Designer or Contentful, whether category landing pages are SFCC-routed or built in Contentful Studio Experiences, and whether the mega-menu includes Contentful-authored promotional tiles. The working assumption is in the ownership table in §1.
137	3. **Contentful Space and per-environment credentials.** Contentful to provide per-environment CDA token, CPA token, Space ID, environment ID, and webhook secret so the storefront can be tested against a real Contentful environment.

Not yet confirmed is the split on composed pages: which editorial blocks appear on PDP and PLP, whether they are authored in SFCC Page Designer or Contentful, whether category landing pages are SFCC-routed or built in Contentful Studio Experiences, and whether the mega-menu includes Contentful-authored promotional tiles. The working assumption is in the ownership table in §1.
3. **Contentful Space and per-environment credentials.** Contentful to provide per-environment CDA token, CPA token, Space ID, environment ID, and webhook secret so the storefront can be tested against a real Contentful environment.

Part 1 — Writing User Stories
-----------------------------

### Before you start

Always go through stories **one at a time**. For each story:

1. **Check the Functional Requirements first** — find the relevant requirement(s) in [04.1 Functional Requirements](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/301793284). The relationship between requirements and stories is flexible: one requirement may map to one story, multiple requirements may be covered by a single story, or one requirement may result in more than one story (e.g. when it needs splitting into frontend and backend). Identify which Req IDs are covered, whether there are any gaps, and whether the story belongs in the right epic.
2. **Check the Personas page** — confirm the correct persona in [04.3 Personas](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/245694470) before drafting. The persona affects who does UAT, what BM permissions are involved, and what training Zimmermann needs post-launch.
3. **Check the epic's squad label in Jira** — look up the parent epic to confirm its `Squad-A` or `Squad-B` label. Don't assume squad ownership from the functional area alone.
4. **Draft, review, move on** — only proceed to the next story once the current one is agreed.

### Prompt template — drafting a single story

Use this to start a story drafting conversation with Claude:

Draft a user story for the SFCC project based on this functional requirement: Req ID: [e.g. HPC-034] Requirement: [paste from the Functional Requirements Confluence page] Area: [e.g. Footer — Navigation] Epic: [epic key or name] Config/Custom: [Custom / Config — from the FR page] Check the Personas page and suggest the right persona. Write acceptance criteria as numbered Given/When/Then statements. List any open items or dependencies with suggested owners where possible. Do not create the story yet — show me the draft first.

Once the draft is approved:

Create this as a Jira story in project SFCC: - Summary: [short title] - Epic: [epic key] - Assignee: me - Functional Area (customfield\_10236): [e.g. PDP / Home Page / PLP / Search / Integration] - Squad (customfield\_10237): [Squad A / Squad B] - Rollout Scope (customfield\_10242): [select all that apply: AU, AE, EU - Domestic, EU - International, HK, UK, US - Domestic, US - International] - Labels: [HPC-034;Custom;Squad-A] - Description: As a [persona], I want [goal], so that [benefit]. [any additional context] - Acceptance Criteria (customfield\_10231): [numbered Given/When/Then statements] - Dependencies (customfield\_10232): [@Name: open item or question] - Priority: [High / Medium / Low]

### Story format

**Summary** — short title only, e.g. `Footer – Join Us Email Capture & Registration Modal`. Do **not** put the "As a / I want / so that" here. Keep it scannable for the backlog.

**Description** — the full user story sentence, followed by any additional context needed for developers or testers. The description must contain only the user story and context — never AC or dependencies:

As a [persona], I want [goal], so that [benefit]. [Any additional context]

**Acceptance Criteria** — always Given/When/Then, numbered for traceability, one criterion per statement. Cover the happy path, edge cases, and negative tests where relevant. Goes in the dedicated **Acceptance Criteria field** (`customfield_10231`), not in the description.

1. Given [context/precondition], when [action], then [expected outcome].
2. Given ...

**Labels** — format: `HPC-034;HPC-035;Custom;Squad-A` — semicolons, no spaces. Always include:

* The Req ID(s) the story covers (from the functional requirements page)
* `Custom` or `Config`
* `Squad-A` or `Squad-B` (taken from the parent epic's label in Jira)

**Functional Area** (`customfield_10236`) — picklist reflecting the functional area of the story. Values in use: `PDP`, `Home Page`, `PLP`, `Search`, `Integration`. Use `Integration` for stories that are primarily about connecting SFCC to an external system, regardless of which epic they sit in.

**Squad** (`customfield_10237`) — set to `Squad A` or `Squad B` based on the parent epic's label in Jira.

**Rollout Scope** (`customfield_10242`) — multi-select checkbox defining which storefronts this story applies to. Select all that apply:

* `AU` — Australia (domestic + Oceania)
* `AE` — Middle East (Global-e)
* `EU - Domestic`
* `EU - International` (Global-e)
* `HK` — Hong Kong (Global-e)
* `UK`
* `US - Domestic`
* `US - International` (Global-e)

If the story applies to all storefronts, select all. If it is storefront-specific (e.g. a Global-e-only integration story), select only the relevant ones.

Note: passing "me" does not resolve via the Jira API — always use the reporter's email address directly instead (the reporter field is auto-populated and can be read from the created issue).

@[Name]: [question or dependency]

**Epic** — always link to the relevant epic. If unsure of the epic key, ask Claude: *"What is the epic key for [area] in project SFCC?"*

**Priority** — High / Medium / Low

### Personas

Always check [04.3 Personas](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/245694470). Common personas:

| Persona | Who |
| --- | --- |
| **Shopper** | End customer browsing/buying |
| **Site Merchandiser** | Business user managing products/content in BM day-to-day |
| **Site Admin** | Technical user doing one-time platform configuration |
| **Developer** | Used for enabler stories (e.g. sample data load) |

### Splitting stories — frontend vs backend

When a requirement involves both a UI component and backend logic (e.g. a form and its integration to an external system, or a product attribute and how it renders on a page), write **two separate stories** — one for the frontend and one for the backend. Different developers typically work on each, even within the same squad.

### Bulk creation

The preferred approach is one story at a time, drafted and reviewed in the Claude chat. When you have a batch of straightforward stories to create at once, bulk creation is also supported — but always review the proposed list before confirming.

Create the following Jira stories in project SFCC, all under epic SFCC-[N], all [priority] priority, all labelled "[label]", assigned to me, Functional Area [value], Squad [A / B], Rollout Scope [list storefronts]: 1. [summary] 2. [summary] 3. [summary] Show me the list before creating anything so I can confirm.

### Sequencing within an epic

Stories should be sequenced so that:

1. **Foundation stories come first** — data model, attribute schema, taxonomy must exist before anything else
2. **Enabler stories unblock downstream work** — e.g. a sample data load story should be sequenced early so other developers can build and test against real data
3. **Integration stories come last** — built against the foundation, tested against sample data first
4. **Flag MuleSoft/third-party dependencies explicitly** in labels and the Dependencies field

### Config vs Custom

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Config** | SFCC out-of-the-box — just needs configuring in Business Manager |
| **Custom** | Requires a custom build (PWA component, custom attribute, custom logic) |

### Scope boundary — Accenture vs Zimmermann

Accenture scope ends at **SFCC platform + PWA Kit + SFCC-side integrations**. Flag the following in open items but do not build:

* MuleSoft development
* GTM / analytics container logic
* Content authoring in Contentful
* Google Merchant feed configuration
* UAT, performance testing, pen-test execution
* BM training and org change management

### API error handling — field failures

When creating a story via the Jira API, individual fields can fail independently. If a field fails:

* **Do not fall back to putting its content in the description.** The description must only ever contain the user story and context.
* **Do not abandon the other fields.** Set all remaining fields correctly in the same create call, then follow up with a separate update call to retry the failed field.
* **Report the failure explicitly** — tell the user which field failed and that it needs to be set manually or will be retried.

The description, AC (`customfield_10231`), and Dependencies (`customfield_10232`) are three separate fields and must always be kept separate, even if a field update fails.

#### Setting customfield\_10231 (Acceptance Criteria) and customfield\_10232 (Dependencies)

These fields must be passed as **plain text strings** via the `additional_fields` parameter — not via the `fields` parameter, and not as ADF (Atlassian Document Format) objects. Passing them as ADF or via `fields` will return an error.

**Correct approach — use `additional_fields` with plain text strings:**

Defaultnoneadditional\_fields: {
"customfield\_10231": "1. Given ... when ... then ...\n2. Given ... when ... then ...",
"customfield\_10232": "@Name: open item or question.\nDepends on SFCC-XX."
}

**Do not do this — passing as ADF object will fail:**

Defaultnonefields: {
"customfield\_10231": { "type": "doc", "version": 1, "content": [...] }
}

**Do not do this — passing via `fields` as plain text will also fail:**

Defaultnonefields: {
"customfield\_10231": "1. Given ..."
}

This applies to both create and update calls. Always set these two fields via `additional_fields` with plain string values.

### Common mistakes

| Situation | Wrong | Right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AC format | Bullet checklist in description | Numbered Given/When/Then in `customfield_10231` |
| AC location | AC written into the description field | AC goes only in `customfield_10231` — never in description |
| AC API call | Passing `customfield_10231` via `fields` or as ADF | Pass via `additional_fields` as a plain text string |
| Dependencies location | Dependencies written into the description field | Dependencies go only in `customfield_10232` — never in description |
| Dependencies API call | Passing `customfield_10232` via `fields` or as ADF | Pass via `additional_fields` as a plain text string |
| Open items | Free text in description | In `customfield_10232`, with owner where possible |
| Labels | `HPC034` or `HPC-034, Custom` | `HPC-034;Custom;Squad-A` (semicolons, no spaces) |
| Squad label | Assumed from functional area | Check the parent epic's label in Jira |
| Functional Area | Left blank | Set `customfield_10236` — use `Integration` for external system stories |
| Squad field | Left blank | Set `customfield_10237` to `Squad A` or `Squad B` |
| Rollout Scope | Left blank | Set `customfield_10242` — select all applicable storefronts |
| Assignee | Left unassigned or passing "me" to the API | Assign at creation time using the reporter's email address directly ("me" does not resolve via the Jira API) |
| Field API failure | Dumping failed field content into description | Set all other fields correctly; retry the failed field separately; report the failure to the user |
| Splitting stories | One story covering UI + integration | Two stories — one frontend, one backend |
| Starting without FRs | Going straight to Jira | Check [04.1 Functional Requirements](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/301793284) first |

Part 2 — Jira Backlog Management
--------------------------------

### Searching the backlog

Show me all open stories in epic SFCC-[N], sorted by priority. Include assignee and status. Show me all stories in project SFCC labelled "checkout" that are not yet started. Show me all Jira stories assigned to me in project SFCC that are In Progress or To Do. Show me all stories in project SFCC updated in the last 7 days. Show me all stories in project SFCC with priority Blocker or Critical that are not Done.

### Updating a story

Update Jira story SFCC-[N]: - Change priority to Critical - Add label: go-live-blocker - Add this to the description under a new heading "Additional Context": [text]

To reassign:

Reassign SFCC-[N] to [name or email]. Add a comment: "Reassigned to [name] per standup [date]."

### Transitioning status

Jira statuses have underlying transition IDs that vary per project. Claude checks available transitions automatically.

Move SFCC-[N] to "In Progress". Move SFCC-[N] to "In Review". Add comment: "PR raised — #[N]. Waiting on QA sign-off." Close SFCC-[N] as Done. Add comment: "Verified in STAGE environment [date]."

Bulk transition:

Move all stories in the current sprint of project SFCC that are "In Review" and have label "[label]" to "Done". Show me the list before changing anything.

### Adding comments

Add a comment to SFCC-[N]: "[text]"

### Linking stories

Link SFCC-[N] to SFCC-[M] as "blocks" — SFCC-[N] blocks SFCC-[M].

### Sprint management

Add stories SFCC-[N], SFCC-[M], SFCC-[O] to the active sprint on the SFCC board. Show me all stories in the active sprint on the SFCC board. Group by status. Include story points if available.

Part 3 — Cross-Cutting Patterns
-------------------------------

### After a workshop

I've just come out of a discovery workshop. Here are my rough notes: [paste notes or transcript excerpt] Do two things: 1. Update Confluence page ID [N] — add today's decisions as a new dated section. 2. Create Jira stories in project SFCC for each open action item. Use epic [key], priority Medium, label "discovery". Show me the proposed stories before creating them.

### Sprint planning from a spec

Here is our sprint planning doc. Extract all items marked [STORY] and create them as Jira stories in project SFCC. Map [EPIC] tags to the corresponding epic keys. Flag anything where the epic key is ambiguous and ask me before creating. [paste doc]

### Status reporting

Give me a status summary for the SFCC project: - Stories completed this week (moved to Done in last 7 days) - Stories currently In Progress with their assignees - Any stories flagged as blocked or with priority Critical/Blocker - Count of stories remaining in the current sprint Format it as a brief update I can paste into a Slack channel.

    "title": "Guide 1: Writing Stories & Acceptance Criteria with Claude",
    "type": "page",
    "created": "",

    "url": "https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/277577757",
    "space": {
      "key": "SFCC",

    },
    "version": 2,

    "content": {
      "value": "> **Who this is for:** Business Analysts
> **Stages covered:** Stage 1 (Story Intake) and Stage 2 (AC Authoring)
> **Prerequisite:** Read the [AI-Assisted QA — Overview & Methodology](../277544962) first.

---

What This Guide Covers
----------------------

This guide explains how to structure a Jira story so that Claude can generate high-quality, Zephyr-ready acceptance criteria (AC) from it — and how to prompt Claude correctly to get output that needs minimal rework.

The output of Stage 2 is a set of approved Given/When/Then acceptance criteria attached to the Jira story, with the story status set to **AC Approved**. Nothing moves to Zephyr until that status is set.

---

Stage 1 — Preparing the Jira Story
----------------------------------

Before you prompt Claude, the story needs to be well-formed. A vague story produces vague AC. Claude is only as good as the context it is given.

### The Story Template

Every Jira story on this programme must follow this structure in the **Description** field:

`**User Role**
[Who is performing this action — e.g. Guest Shopper, Registered Customer, Merchandiser]
**Goal**
[What they are trying to achieve — one sentence, from the user's perspective]
**Context / Trigger**
[What situation or action leads to this flow — e.g. "Customer has added items to cart and proceeds to checkout"]
**In Scope**
[What this story explicitly covers — be specific. List the flows, states, or interactions this story is responsible for.]
**Out of Scope**
[What this story does NOT cover — prevents AC from bleeding into adjacent stories]
**Regions**
[Which storefronts this story applies to — AU / UK / US DOM / US INTL / EU DOM / EU INTL / ME — or ALL]
**Edge Cases to Consider**
[Anything you already know about — empty states, validation errors, unavailable services, regional variants]
**Jira Story Key**
[The story key — e.g. ZIM-042 — used in test case naming]`

### What Good Looks Like — Example

`**User Role**
Guest Shopper
**Goal**
Complete a domestic checkout as a guest without creating an account
**Context / Trigger**
Customer has one or more items in their bag and clicks "Checkout" on the bag page.
Storefront: AU (SFCC domestic checkout, Adyen payment, Avalara tax for NZ addresses only)
**In Scope**
- Full checkout journey: contact details → shipping address → shipping method → payment → order confirmation
- Adyen card payment only (Apple Pay / Google Pay out of scope for this story — see ZIM-044)
- Error handling: invalid card, declined card, address validation failure
- Post-order: confirmation page renders with order number; confirmation email triggers
**Out of Scope**
- Registered customer checkout (see ZIM-043)
- Express checkout / Apple Pay / Google Pay (see ZIM-044)
- International checkout via Global-e (see ZIM-051)
- Post-checkout account creation prompt (see ZIM-048)
**Regions**
AU only
**Edge Cases to Consider**
- Card declined by Adyen
- Card number fails Luhn validation before submission
- Shipping address outside AU (should not be reachable on AU storefront — confirm behaviour)
- Didomi consent not given — confirm GTM purchase event does not fire
**Jira Story Key**
ZIM-042`

---

Stage 2 — Prompting Claude to Write AC
--------------------------------------

### The Prompt Template

Once your story is ready, open Claude (claude.ai) and use this prompt. Copy the entire block and fill in the bracketed sections.

`You are writing acceptance criteria for a Jira story on the Zimmermann SFCC replatform —
a Magento 2 to Salesforce Commerce Cloud migration using PWA Kit on Managed Runtime,
with Adyen (domestic payments), Global-e (international checkout), Contentful (CMS),
and MuleSoft (integration layer).
Here is the story:
---
[PASTE YOUR FULL STORY DESCRIPTION HERE]
---
Please write acceptance criteria using the Given/When/Then format. For each criterion:
- Write one scenario per test case (not compound scenarios)
- Use plain English — no technical jargon unless it is the correct term (e.g. "Adyen", "Didomi")
- Cover: the happy path, all error paths in the In Scope section, and the edge cases listed
- For each scenario, specify the region it applies to in brackets at the end — e.g. [AU] [ALL] [EU DOM + EU INTL]
- Do not invent scope — if something is listed as Out of Scope, do not write AC for it
- Number each acceptance criterion sequentially: AC-01, AC-02, etc.
Format each criterion as:
**AC-[N]: [Short descriptive title]** [REGION]
**Given** [precondition]
**When** [action]
**Then** [expected outcome]
**And** [additional expected outcomes if needed]`

### What Claude Will Produce

Claude will return a numbered list of AC in the Given/When/Then format, one per scenario, tagged by region. A well-formed story typically produces between 6 and 15 AC items — fewer usually means edge cases were missed, more usually means the story scope is too wide.

### Example Output (partial)

`**AC-01: Guest completes checkout with a valid card** [AU]
**Given** a guest shopper has one or more items in their bag
**When** they complete all checkout steps and submit a valid Adyen card
**Then** an order is created and the confirmation page displays the order number
**And** an order confirmation email is triggered
**AC-04: Card declined at payment step** [AU]
**Given** a guest shopper has reached the payment step of checkout
**When** they submit a card that Adyen declines
**Then** an inline error message is displayed at the payment step
**And** the customer remains on the payment step with their details retained
**And** the order is not created
**AC-07: GTM purchase event suppressed when consent not given** [AU]
**Given** a guest shopper has completed checkout
**And** they have not accepted analytics cookies via Didomi
**When** the order confirmation page loads
**Then** the GTM purchase event does not fire`

---

Reviewing and Approving AC
--------------------------

This is the most important step. Claude's output is a first draft. You must read every criterion before approving.

### Review Checklist

Work through each AC item and ask:

* **Is the precondition (Given) accurate?** Does it match the actual state the user would be in?
* **Is the action (When) specific enough?** "Submits the form" is better than "clicks a button" — but "clicks the Place Order button" is better still when the element is specific.
* **Is the outcome (Then) testable?** "The order is created" is testable. "The experience is good" is not.
* **Is the region tag correct?** An AU-only story should not have AC tagged [ALL].
* **Are edge cases covered?** Check the story's Edge Cases section against the AC list.
* **Is anything missing?** Common gaps: empty state when a list returns no results, service degradation (e.g. Didomi unavailable), accessibility (keyboard navigation, screen reader text).
* **Is anything out of scope included?** Remove or redirect to the correct story.

### Iterating with Claude

If the output needs changes, give Claude specific corrections rather than asking it to "redo" the whole thing:

* "AC-03 is missing the case where the address validation API is unavailable — add a degradation criterion."
* "AC-07 applies to EU DOM and EU INTL as well as AU. Update the region tag."
* "Combine AC-08 and AC-09 — they are the same scenario."

Claude maintains context within the conversation, so you can iterate without re-pasting the full story.

### Setting the Jira Status

Once you are satisfied with the AC:

1. Copy the approved AC into the **Acceptance Criteria** field on the Jira story (or the Description if your project uses that field)
2. Set the story status to **AC Approved**
3. Comment on the Jira story: `AC approved [your name] [date]`

The story is now ready for Stage 3 — Zephyr test case creation.

---

Common Mistakes to Avoid
------------------------

| Mistake | Why It Matters | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vague "When" step — "user proceeds with checkout" | Cannot be automated — the test runner needs to know what to click | Name the specific action: "clicks the Proceed to Payment button" |
| Compound Then — "order is created and email sends and page renders" | One failure masks the others in test results | Split into separate And clauses or separate AC items |
| Missing region tag | Tester doesn't know whether to run on all storefronts or one | Always tag, even if the answer is [ALL] |
| AC covers Out of Scope items | Creates ambiguity about what the story is responsible for | Delete and note the correct story key |
| Approving without reading | Claude drafts; the BA is accountable for the approved AC | Read every criterion — this is the human gate |

---

Quick Reference — AC Status Flow
--------------------------------

`Story drafted by BA
│
▼
Claude generates AC draft
│
▼
BA reviews and edits ──► iterate with Claude if needed
│
▼
BA approves — sets Jira status to AC Approved ◀ HUMAN GATE 1
│
▼
Story ready for Stage 3 — Zephyr test case creation`

---

*Last updated: June 2026 | Zimmermann Digital Modernisation — Accenture Song*",

I'm seeing two distinct component patterns here. The entry-driven components in the Contentful directory accept typed Contentful entries or assets as props, pulling their data shape directly from the content model. These components leverage Live Preview by passing the entry ID, field ID, and locale to get real-time updates—so the Contentful content model itself is the source of truth for the data contract.

The Studio Experiences components, by contrast, use flat scalar props annotated with `@cf` that get code-generated into `definitions.ts`.
